chunks: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutawakkil - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashem quoted on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, on the authority of Muqatil ibn Muqatil, who said: 'I saw Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) on'

a Friday at noon while he was in the state of ritual consecration (Ihram) and performing phlebotomy (Hijamah) at the roadside.' The author of this book - may God have mercy upon him - said regarding this hadith: 'There are benefits. The first is the permissibility of phlebotomy on Friday when needed, and it should be known that what has been reported regarding its dislike applies only in the case of choice (non-necessity). The second benefit is the permissibility of phlebotomy at the time of noon. The third benefit is that it is permissible for the one in Ihram to perform phlebotomy if he is compelled, and he should not shave the place of phlebotomy.'

key_terms.الِاخْتِيَار: Choice or optionality (as opposed to necessity)
key_terms.عِنْدَ الضَّرُورَة: When needed or out of necessity
key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: One in the state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.وَقْتِ الزَّوَال: The time of noon (when the sun begins to decline)

ai.seo_question: What are the rulings for phlebotomy (cupping) for a person in Ihram and on Friday?
ai.summary: This narration from *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida* highlights Imam al-Rida’s (a) practice of cupping during Ihram, serving as a primary evidence for the permissibility of medical procedures that involve minor hair removal without breaking the pilgrimage state. The author, Shaykh al-Saduq, clarifies that the general dislike of Friday cupping applies only to voluntary cases, emphasizing the principle of necessity (darura) in Islamic jurisprudence. This incident underscores the flexibility of Shia fiqh in balancing ritual purity with practical health needs during the sacred months.
